questions_and_answers.question_text: What are the two meanings of tài?
Which word is búguò often interchangeable with?
What does kǒngpà mean, and what else may it sometimes mean?
What is the key difference between a manner adverb expression and a compound verb of result?
How many parts does a compound verb of result always have?

answers.answer_text: There are always three, and only three, parts.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "Not only can he speak Chinese, but he can also speak Japanese."

answers.answer_text: Tā búdàn huì shuō Zhōngwén, yě huì shuō Rìwén.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Which verb indicates the result in tīngbudǒng?
Write the Chinese for "This book is probably his."
Can a compound verb of result take additional adverbs like hěn or tài?

answers.answer_text: No — only manner adverb expressions can expand that way.

articles.text:
3. B: Nà tài hǎo le!                That's wonderful!
   B: Hěn xīwàng gēn ta tántan.     I wish very much to talk with her.
   B: Búguò, kǒngpà wǒde Yīngwén    However, I'm afraid that my English
      bù xíng.                       isn't good enough.
   B: Búdàn shuōde bù hǎo, yǒu      Not only don't I speak well, but
      shíhou yě tīngbudǒng.          sometimes I can't understand what
                                     I hear either.

Notes on No. 3

Tài hǎo le, "wonderful," or, more literally, "too good." You have seen tài translated as "excessively," or "too." In other contexts, tài simply indicates an extreme degree and is translated as "very." When used this way, tài is commonly heavily stressed.

Zhèiběn shū zhēn shi tài yǒu     This book is really very interesting!
yìsi le!

Búguò, "however," is often interchangeable with kěshi, "but," and is therefore used more frequently than the English "however."

Kǒngpà means "to be afraid that (something is/is not the case)." It sometimes means "probably," as in Zhèiběn shū kǒngpà shi tāde, "This book is probably his."

Búdàn...yě... is equivalent to the English "not only...but also...."

Tā búdàn huì shuō Zhōngwén,      Not only can he speak Chinese, but he
yě huì shuō Rìwén.               can also speak Japanese.
Tā búdàn bù xǐhuan hóngde,       Not only doesn't he like the red one,
yě bù xǐhuan lánde.              but he doesn't like the blue one
                                 either.

Tīngbudǒng, "can't understand": The verb dǒng is used to indicate the result in a compound verb of result.

Zhōngwén bàozhǐ nǐ kàndedǒng     Can you read (and understand) Chinese
kànbudǒng?                       newspapers?

Shuōde bù hǎo VS. tīngbudǒng: The many ways in which one-syllable Chinese verbs may be combined to make patterns and compounds can be confusing. In No. 3, you see both an action verb and its manner adverb (in the negative), shuōde bù hǎo, and a compound verb of result (in its "unable" form), tīngbudǒng. Compare these two forms:

ACTION VERB | MARKER | NEG. | ADV. | MANNER      (manner adverb)
shuō        | -de    | bù   |      | hǎo
shuō        | -de    |      | hěn  | hǎo

ACTION VERB | MARKER or NEG. (not both) | RESULT  (compound verb of result)
tīng        | -bu-                      | -dǒng
tīng        | -de-                      | -dǒng

The marker de is always part of the manner adverb expression but alternates with bu in compound verbs of result. Manner adverb expressions expand to allow not only for negation but also for additional adverbs such as hěn and tài. Compound verbs of result cannot do this. There are always three, and only three, parts to the compound verb of result.
